name: Problem Definition
definition: A precise statement of the problem a project will solve, who is affected, its scope, its constraints and its success criteria.
example: Members cannot see which courts are free, so a court is sometimes booked twice.

name: Project Management
definition: The process of planning, organising, controlling resources, monitoring timelines and activities, and completing a project to achieve a goal that meets identified criteria.
example: A team uses a Gantt chart and a process diary to keep a six-week booking system on schedule.

name: Milestone
definition: An important point in a project, shown as a hollow diamond on a Gantt chart, that marks the completion of a phase or an approval and has no duration.
example: The milestone "Requirements approved" is reached when the club committee signs off the needs list.

name: Critical Path
definition: The longest chain of dependent tasks in a project, which decides the earliest finish date, so a delay to any task on it delays the whole project.
example: If the database build slips a day, the dependent screens, integration and testing all move back a day.

name: Scope Creep
definition: The gradual addition of extra features or requirements to a project without matching changes to time, budget or resources.
example: A club asks for online payments halfway through a six-week booking project.

name: Iterative Development
definition: Repeating a cycle of design, build, test and review so that each pass improves the system using feedback.
example: A paper prototype of a booking screen is tested, redrawn and tested again before any code is written.

name: Waterfall (Structured) Approach
definition: A development approach in which stages such as requirements, design, development and testing run in order, each completed and approved before the next begins.
example: A hospital records system with fixed regulatory requirements is developed in signed-off stages.

name: Agile Approach
definition: A development approach that builds the system in short cycles, each producing working output that the client reviews before the next cycle is planned.
example: A team delivers bookings in a first two-week sprint and canteen stock in the second.

name: Minimum Viable Product
definition: The simplest version of a product that solves the core problem and can be tested with real users.
example: A start-up releases a booking page for one club before adding payments or reports.

name: End-User Development
definition: A development approach in which the people who will use the system build it themselves, usually with tools such as spreadsheets or no-code software.
example: A club secretary builds a membership tracker in a spreadsheet.

name: Outsourcing
definition: Contracting an outside organisation to develop a system or part of it, wherever that organisation is located.
example: A council pays a software company to build its permits system to an agreed specification.

name: Offshore Development
definition: Having a system built by a team in another country, either in the organisation's own overseas office or in a contracted firm.
example: An Australian retailer has its online shop maintained by a development team overseas.

name: Freelance Work
definition: Work done by a self-employed person who takes on tasks or projects for one or more clients rather than being an employee.
example: A club hires a freelance designer to create the screens for its booking system.

name: Feasibility Study
definition: An assessment, made before a project is committed to, of whether it can succeed technically, economically, operationally, on schedule and legally.
example: A team checks that the planned cost is within budget and that volunteers can be trained before starting the build.

name: Risk Register
definition: A record of the identified risks to a project, with each risk's likelihood, impact, response and owner.
example: A register lists "key team member unavailable" as high risk with a response of pairing on critical tasks.

name: Contingency
definition: An amount of money or time set aside in a plan to cover problems that could not be foreseen.
example: A budget of $690 adds a 10% contingency of $69.

name: Change Request
definition: A formal request to alter something already agreed, assessed for its effect on cost, time and scope before it is accepted.
example: The committee asks for a waiting list and the team costs it before agreeing to add it.

name: Regression Testing
definition: Repeating earlier tests after a change to confirm that nothing that previously worked has been broken.
example: After fixing the 120-minute limit, the team also retests the 29, 30 and 120 minute cases.

name: Boundary Data
definition: Test values that lie on and immediately either side of a limit in a rule.
example: For a 30 to 120 minute booking, the boundary values are 29, 30, 120 and 121.

name: Erroneous Data
definition: Test data that the system should reject, such as the wrong type, an impossible value or a missing entry.
example: Entering "abc" or a blank for a booking length.

name: Operation Documentation
definition: Instructions for the people who use a system day to day, such as a user guide or quick-reference card.
example: A laminated card showing the canteen coordinator how to record a stock count.

name: Maintenance Documentation
definition: Technical information for the people who look after a system, covering its design, configuration, backup and update procedures and a log of changes.
example: A guide that shows a committee member how to restore last night's backup.

name: System Implementation
definition: NESA: the implementation method applied when introducing a new or redesigned enterprise system, typically direct, parallel, phased or pilot.
example: A club goes live with its stock module first and its booking module three weeks later.

name: Stakeholder
definition: A person or group who is affected by a project or has an interest in its outcome.
example: Members, the club secretary, the canteen coordinator and suppliers are stakeholders in a booking and inventory system.
